title: the rule that keeps turning up
hook: the rule that keeps turning up
tomorrow: why a sound starts and ends a sit

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: notice. Your line: where is it right now? So where was it, most of yesterday? No grade. Just the answer. Day four.

A playground, right after somebody grabbed something that wasn't theirs. A grown-up crouches down and says it: treat people the way you want to be treated. Plenty of kids hear it before they can read. It's so familiar it sounds like nothing. But here's the strange part. You can find it in ancient China. In the Hebrew Bible. In the sayings of the rabbis. In the Gospels. In India's great epic, the Mahabharata. In Greek writers. It turns up on path after path. Today's word is the golden rule.
screen: `TREAT PEOPLE THE WAY YOU WANT TO BE TREATED.` → `CHINA. THE BIBLE. INDIA. GREECE.` → `PATH AFTER PATH.`

segments.voice: Start in China, with the Analects, the sayings of Confucius. A student asks Confucius if there's one word you could live by your whole life. In James Legge's translation of the Analects, Confucius answers: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Notice it's a don't. Then the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus, in among laws about harvests and fair wages, comes the line the King James renders: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The Talmud tells of a man who asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel says, roughly: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it. Then Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount, puts it as a do: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." India's Mahabharata has a version. So does the Greek orator Isocrates. Did each path arrive at it on its own? Nobody can say for sure who heard what from whom. What's clear is that it keeps turning up, and each tradition keeps it in its own place. For Confucius it's one word for a whole life. For Hillel, a summary that sends you back to study. For Jesus, in Matthew's words, "this is the law and the prophets." The name, the golden rule, came much later than any of them. One more thing. The rule starts with you. What you don't want. What you would want. It asks you to use your own heart as a map of someone else's.
screen: `CONFUCIUS: RECIPROCITY.` · `LEVITICUS: YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `HILLEL: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` · `JESUS: DO YE EVEN SO TO THEM.` · then, large: `YOUR HEART AS A MAP OF SOMEONE ELSE'S.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first breath, think of someone you'll see today. On the second, ask: if I were them, today, what would I want? Maybe to be listened to. Maybe to be left alone for a bit. Maybe just a real hello. On the third breath, let the answer settle. You don't have to do anything yet. Just know it.
The golden rule. What you'd want, given. What you'd hate, held back. Found on path after path. Fourth word.
Your line: be good to people. Today, one person, one time: give them the thing you figured out on the second breath. Small is fine. Day four.

howItsDone: The golden rule is taught in many religious and ethical settings: Jewish teaching often recalls Hillel's saying, Christian teaching the Sermon on the Mount, Confucian teaching the Analects, and families often pass it to children as an early rule.

fork.setup: a man asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what does Hillel do?
options: sums it up in one line, then says: go and learn.
fork.reveal: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary; go and learn. in the Talmud's story, another rabbi, Shammai, had already sent the man away.

original.note: Chinese, shu: Confucius's one word for a whole life (Analects 15:23). Legge translates it reciprocity.

trapdoor: what it means: use what you'd want as the map for what you give.
what a scholar hears: Confucius's word is shu (恕); Hillel calls his version the whole Torah (Shabbat 31a); Matthew 7:12 adds "for this is the law and the prophets."

notes: The index title 'the rule that keeps turning up' overclaims; the script tests it honestly ('some probably did; for others, nobody can say who heard what from whom'). Owner may want the index softened.
Legge's Analects 15:23 wording, including the capitals in RECIPROCITY, should be checked against the 1861 edition.
'The golden rule' as a name: English, 17th century. Confirm the date phrasing ('around the 1600s').
Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva 113.8) and Isocrates (Nicocles 61) references: confirm verse numbering.
Hillel story paraphrased (Shabbat 31a); Shammai's refusal appears only in the fork reveal.
